The Broad-toothed tailless bat, Anoura latidens, is a small nectarivorous phyllostomid inhabiting montane cloud forests of the northern Andes. A key aspect of its energetic physiology is its basal metabolic rate, measured through respirometry trials under controlled laboratory conditions. At a resting body temperature characteristic of torpor avoidance in this species, 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], the maximum basal metabolic rate is 21.90 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 21.90 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value aligns closely with predictions for a mammal of this body size and feeding guild, reflecting the high energetic costs of hovering flight and a diet of dilute nectar. The measurement was obtained from post-absorptive, resting individuals during their inactive phase, ensuring that the recorded oxygen consumption represented true basal conditions rather than the elevated rates seen during activity. Such data are critical for understanding how this species partitions energy between maintenance, thermoregulation, and the demands of reproduction in a relatively cool, resource-poor montane environment.

Adult females of Anoura latidens reach a maximum recorded body mass of approximately 18 grams [Wwi = approximately 18 grams], a value that places them among the smaller members of the genus Anoura. This ultimate wet weight is attained after several months of post-weaning growth and is maintained throughout the reproductive lifespan. The female mass is crucial for understanding reproductive investment, as it constrains the size of the offspring she can produce. Based on allometric scaling from a congeneric species, the wet weight at birth is estimated at 4.5 grams [Wwb = 4.5 grams], a relatively large neonate compared to many insectivorous bats of similar adult size. This substantial birth mass likely reflects the advanced developmental state of the newborn, which must be capable of clinging to the mother during nightly foraging trips shortly after parturition. The ratio of birth mass to maternal mass is high, indicating a significant energetic investment by the female during gestation.

Under typical body temperature conditions of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], female Anoura latidens give birth to a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], producing just one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year]. This low reproductive output, typical of many small neotropical bats, is balanced by a relatively high survival rate of offspring and extended maternal care. Gestation lasts a substantial 122 days [tg = 122 days] at the same body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a duration that is long for a bat of this size and suggests a slow pace of foetal development. The prolonged gestation may be an adaptation to the unpredictable nectar availability in montane habitats, allowing the female to spread the energetic costs of pregnancy over a longer period. Following parturition, the pup is entirely dependent on milk, which provides a rich source of lipids and proteins necessary for rapid growth.

The early life of a newborn Anoura latidens is characterized by complete dependence on maternal care. The time from birth to weaning, when the juvenile achieves nutritional independence, is estimated at 30.5 days [tx = 30.5 days] at a maternal body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. During this suckling stage, the pup grows rapidly, increasing its body mass several-fold as it develops the flight muscles and skeletal structure necessary for sustained flight. Weaning marks a critical transition to a diet of nectar and pollen, which requires the development of specialized foraging skills and a digestive system capable of processing plant exudates. The relatively short weaning period compared to gestation is typical for bats, as the milk is highly nutritious and the young grow quickly. After weaning, the juvenile enters a sub-adult phase of independent foraging and continued somatic growth.

Sexual maturity in Anoura latidens, defined as the attainment of full reproductive capability, is reached at approximately 365 days after birth [tp = approximately 365 days after birth], occurring at a body temperature of 38.5 °C [T = 38.5 °C] during active periods. This age at puberty, roughly one year, is consistent with that of other small phyllostomid bats and reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over early reproduction. Following puberty, females may not breed immediately, as they must first establish a home range and secure access to reliable nectar resources. The maximum lifespan for this species is estimated at around 10 years [am = around 10 years] at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C], a relatively extended longevity for a bat of this small body size and typical of the low extrinsic mortality rates found in tropical species, likely resulting in a long reproductive window during which a female can produce multiple litters over her lifetime.
